Blue Ocean Strategy: C1 Lesson

C1 ESL Connect Video lesson based on the tapescript: red oceans, blue oceans, Cirque du Soleil, value innovation and market creation.

Video link: Open on YouTube

Lesson Aim

Analyse how Cirque du Soleil changed what customers were willing to pay for. Use the case to distinguish market creation from competition for existing demand and evaluate whether the strategy could be replicated.

Before watching

  1. What makes a market highly competitive?
  2. Can a company succeed by avoiding direct competition?
  3. What industries have created completely new customer demand?

Comprehension 1

Click each question to reveal the answer.

What was surprising about Cirque du Soleil’s success?
It grew while the circus business was in long-term decline
What do red oceans represent?
Existing industries with clear competition
What do companies try to do in red oceans?
Outperform rivals and grab existing demand
What happens as the competitive space gets crowded?
Competition becomes fierce
Why is the decline of the traditional circus important to the argument about Cirque du Soleil?
It makes general industry growth an unlikely explanation for Cirque’s success. That contrast supports looking at how its offer differed from what established circuses were selling.

Comprehension 2

Click each question to reveal the answer.

What is a blue ocean strategy about?
Creating and capturing unknown markets
How did Cirque du Soleil alter the circus industry?
It blurred the line between circus and theatre
Which customers did Cirque attract?
Adults prepared to pay premium ticket prices
What did Cirque eliminate from the traditional circus?
Costly animal acts and star performers
How did Cirque change both what customers valued and what the company paid for?
It added theatrical elements that appealed to adults willing to pay premium prices and removed costly elements such as animal acts and star performers.

C1 Grammar · Cleft Sentences and Inversion

Cleft sentences

Use a cleft to bring one part of a message into focus.

  • It-cleft: It was the theatrical staging that set the show apart. The focus follows it was.
  • What-cleft: What set the show apart was its theatrical staging. The what clause introduces the topic and the information after was carries the focus.

Inversion after negative or restrictive openings

After fronted expressions such as rarely, not only, and only by, put the auxiliary before the subject. Add do, does, or did when the original clause has no auxiliary. After not until, invert the main clause: Not until the market became crowded did the company reconsider its strategy.

Rewrite for a strategy briefing

Keep the original meaning and use the opening given. Select an item to reveal its model answer.

1. Begin with “It was” to emphasise the change. The move towards theatre helped Cirque stand out.

It was the move towards theatre that helped Cirque stand out.

2. Begin with “It was” to emphasise the audience. Cirque attracted adults who were willing to pay higher ticket prices.

It was adults who were willing to pay higher ticket prices that Cirque attracted.

3. Begin with “What”. Cirque changed the kind of experience the audience could expect.

What Cirque changed was the kind of experience the audience could expect.

4. Begin with “What Cirque did”. Cirque cut costly acts and added theatrical elements.

What Cirque did was cut costly acts and add theatrical elements.

5. Begin with “Rarely”. Established companies rarely rethink the boundaries of their industry.

Rarely do established companies rethink the boundaries of their industry.

6. Begin with “Not only”. Cirque removed costly acts and attracted a new audience.

Not only did Cirque remove costly acts, but it also attracted a new audience.

7. Begin with “Only by”. The team could test demand only by offering a trial performance.

Only by offering a trial performance could the team test demand.

8. Begin with “Not until”. The managers understood the appeal of the new format only after they saw how audiences responded.

Not until they saw how audiences responded did the managers understand the appeal of the new format.

Thought-Provoking Questions

1. Is it better to compete in an existing market or create a new one?

2. Can every company create a blue ocean?

3. Why are blue ocean strategies hard for rivals to copy?

4. What risks come with changing industry boundaries?

5. What other companies have created new market space?

6. Is low cost always compatible with differentiation?

7. How could a small business apply Blue Ocean Strategy?

Context

Situation: A traditional entertainment company is losing customers. The leadership team wants to redesign the business model.

Student A

You are a strategy consultant. Explain how the company can create a blue ocean by changing industry boundaries.

Student B

You are the CEO. Ask about risks, costs, customer demand and how competitors might respond.

Role play task: Agree on one element to eliminate, one to reduce, one to raise and one to create.
